title: The Harvest of Harrow Glen
premise: Juniper Lockridge hosts a late-night call-in show in the dying town of Harrow Glen, where a listener named Maren calls in to confess she died six days ago—and every caller after her is someone he knows to be buried. When an excavation crew at the old Lockridge farm unearths a cellar door sealed from the inside, Juniper learns his family's radio tower was never broadcasting to the town; it was answering something beneath it. The dead aren't haunting him—they're warning him that whatever was invited in by his great-grandfather's first broadcast has finished its long patience and wants the last Lockridge to open the door from the outside. Juniper survives sunrise only by doing what no Lockridge ever dared: telling the truth on air, breaking the invitation, and letting the town finally hear what it spent a century refusing to.
about_author: P. M. Lockridge is the pen name of a former small-market radio producer who spent seven years working overnight shifts in towns the highway maps forgot. They write horror about places that keep secrets out of loyalty rather than malice.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. During his 2 a.m. show, a caller named Maren chats amiably about weather, then mentions her funeral was Tuesday. Juniper assumes a prank until he checks the obituaries. The emotional beat is dry professional skepticism cracking into unease; he keeps broadcasting because going silent feels like admitting something.

chapters.title: The Obituary Page
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. He confirms Maren Halvorsen died of exposure near the Glen's edge, then takes three more calls—each a dead local, each polite, each asking if he's 'still keeping the light on.' His producer Dale hears nothing but static. Beat: isolation deepening as the impossible becomes private.

chapters.title: Excavation at the Old Place
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, with crew foreman Ruthie Vasquez. The county crew digging foundations for a cell upgrade on the derelict Lockridge farm strikes a stone lintel—a door set into a hillside cellar, bolted from within. Ruthie asks Juniper, as nominal landowner, whether to proceed. Beat: dread disguised as bureaucratic annoyance.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Kept
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV in the attic of his late grandmother's house: ledgers of nightly broadcast logs dating to 1923, each signed off with the phrase 'invitation maintained.' A photograph shows his great-grandfather Ezra beside the tower, mouth open mid-word. Beat: inheritance revealed as obligation, not property.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. On air, a new caller speaks in Ezra's cadence, thanking him for 'keeping the line warm' and noting the door is nearly clear. When Juniper drives to the farm, the excavation equipment sits abandoned, engines cold, keys gone. Beat: the threat acquires a voice and a schedule.

chapters.title: Ruthie's Report
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. She recounts the dig day: how the soil around the door was soft, turned recently, as if something had been pacing behind it; how her best driller quit mid-shift saying the ground 'answered back.' She warns Juniper to condemn the site. Beat: an outsider's rational testimony making the irrational undeniable.

chapters.title: Loyal Listeners
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The dead callers begin coordinating—one gives him a message from his grandmother: 'Don't let them finish the sentence.' He realizes the dead aren't the threat; they're the previous generation of Lockridges, bound to warn him. Beat: loyalty redefined—the dead are loyal to him, not to the family secret.

chapters.title: The Town That Knew
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV confronting town elder Cora Bright. She admits Harrow Glen has always known: the tower's hum kept something fed and contained, and every family paid a quiet tithe of silence. 'We didn't lie to you, Juniper. We just never told you true.' Beat: belonging exposed as complicity.

chapters.title: Static Between Stations
chapters.summary: Dale's POV. The producer, spooked, plays back old tapes and finds a second voice under sixty years of broadcasts—patient, syllabic, learning words one season at a time. It has been practicing speech through the tower. Beat: horror of realization that the show itself was the lesson plan.

chapters.title: The Door From Inside
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV at the farm at dusk. Through the stone he hears scratching—not frantic but deliberate, like handwriting. The bolts inside shift a fraction each night. His grandmother's final log entry reads: 'It cannot open it. Only we can. That is the mercy. That is the trap.' Beat: agency and guilt converging.

chapters.title: Maren's Last Request
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Maren calls one final time, lucid, explaining the dead can hold the door shut only while someone living speaks to them honestly—his broadcasts have been unknowingly feeding their strength. But the thing below has learned to imitate voices, including hers. Beat: trust fraying; he must discern truth from mimicry.

chapters.title: The Imitation Game
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Two callers claiming to be Maren argue on air. He devises a test—asking about a private grief she confessed in chapter one—and one voice falters. The false one laughs with Ezra's laugh. Beat: triumph curdling into terror as the entity reveals how much it has learned.

chapters.title: Cut the Tower
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. She and her remaining crew offer to topple the transmission tower, severing the entity's channel. Juniper refuses: the logs suggest the signal doesn't just feed it—it pins it. Cut the tower and nothing holds the door but flesh. Beat: the rational solution revealed as catastrophic.

chapters.title: Cora's Confession
chapters.summary: Cora's POV. She tells the full history: in 1923, Ezra Lockridge, grieving and half-mad, broadcast an open invitation to 'anything listening' to come comfort his dead daughter. Something came. The town's silence since has been the price of not being next. Beat: sympathy for complicity; the theme of loyalty vs. truth made explicit.

chapters.title: Nightfall, Night One
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The excavation trench collapses inward; the door stands exposed to open air for the first time in a century. The dead callers go silent one by one, like lights failing. Dale stays at the station, terrified but present. Beat: siege begins; loneliness broken by chosen company.

chapters.title: Voices in the Walls
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV through the night at the station. Every phone line rings with voices he loves—his dead mother, his grandmother—each urging him toward the farm, each slightly wrong in cadence. He holds the line by speaking only truths aloud, refusing even comforting lies. Beat: endurance as moral act.

chapters.title: Dale's Choice
chapters.summary: Dale's POV. The entity offers Dale a bargain—his comatose father's voice, alive again, if he opens the studio transmitter and lets the signal die. Dale nearly does it, hand on the breaker, then instead plays the archive tape of the false voice over the air, exposing the mimicry publicly. Beat: loyalty choosing truth over love's counterfeit.

chapters.title: The Sentence Finished
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. At 4 a.m. the deception fails and the thing drops pretense entirely, speaking in its own voice through every speaker in town: Ezra's invitation, ninety-nine years spoken in fragments, needs only the last word—which only a Lockridge can say. The bolts begin sliding. Beat: climax pressure; the trap's mechanism fully revealed.

chapters.title: Sunrise Broadcast
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Rather than flee or submit, he goes on air and tells everything—Ezra's grief, the town's silence, the door, the mimicry—naming the invitation plainly so it can be refused openly. The dead callers return, adding their voices, a hundred honest testimonies drowning the single false one. Beat: truth as weapon; community forged through confession.

chapters.title: The Word Unsaid
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV at the farm at dawn. The door strains, the last bolt bending, and the entity offers him his mother's true voice as final temptation. He answers with the refusal the town speaks together over the airwaves—an un-invitation—and the bolt snaps outward into silence. Beat: climax resolution; the cost is that everyone now knows everything.

chapters.title: After the Signal
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, weeks later. The tower comes down voluntarily; the show ends; some townsfolk shun him for shattering the comfortable silence, others thank him. Maren's voice comes once more, faintly, saying goodbye without asking anything. Beat: bittersweet belonging—he lost the invisible life but gained a real one.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Juniper's POV. He records a final solo broadcast from the empty station: not a show, just a man telling the truth to whoever might be listening, ending with 'the invitation is closed.' In the last line, far underground, something patient begins—very quietly—to learn a new word. Beat: resolution with a held breath; horror's long memory.
